Jesus teaches his disciples to pray (verses 1–4)

“Lord, teach us to pray” is a good and necessary request.

Only Jesus can truly teach us how to pray, through his word and Spirit.

Lord, teach me what prayer means, awaken in me the desire to pray and show me what I should ask and say.

Jesus gave the disciples a prayer very similar to the one he had taught in the Sermon on the Mount.

Matthew and Luke use slightly different wording, but Henry considers those differences unimportant to the prayer's meaning.

When praying for others and ourselves, we should approach our heavenly Father, trusting his goodness and power.

Jesus encourages perseverance in prayer (verses 5–13)

Jesus encourages us to pray earnestly and continually.

We should ask for what we truly need, as someone asks a kind neighbor for bread.

If God does not immediately answer our requests, we should not give up. He will act in his appointed time.

Especially, ask for the Holy Spirit.

We need his help to pray well, but also because all spiritual blessings are included in that one great gift.

Through the Spirit we come to know God and ourselves, repent, believe in Christ and love him. We find comfort in this life and are prepared for the happiness of the next.

Our Father is more willing to give spiritual blessings to those who ask than a loving human parent is to give food to a hungry child.

Faithful prayer quiets and steadies the heart in God.

Jesus defeats the devil's power and warns against empty reform (verses 14–26)

Casting out demons showed Jesus destroying the power of evil spirits.

Henry compares an unconverted heart to a palace where Satan exercises authority.

There can be a counterfeit peace in such a heart: a sinner feels perfectly safe, has no doubt about spiritual standing and has no fear of coming judgment.

True conversion changes everything.

It is Christ's victory over the devil's rule in a soul, restoring freedom and bringing the mind and body into service to Christ.

But a hypocrite may have a house that looks swept and decorated without being cleansed.

A sinner may confess unwillingly like Pharaoh, show false sorrow like Ahab, or carry out only a partial reform like Herod.

Such changes sweep up loose dirt while leaving a favorite sin untouched.

Outward virtues, abilities and religious appearances are decorations, not true grace.

A heart never given to Christ and never inhabited by the Holy Spirit remains unrenewed.

We should never be satisfied with an outward religion that someone may possess while still falling short of heaven.

Without Christ, the evil spirits return readily and resume their power.

May we seek real deliverance from this dreadful condition.

Those who obey God's word are blessed (verses 27 and 28)

The scribes and Pharisees insulted Jesus' teaching, but a woman marveled at the wisdom and power of his words.

Jesus directed her attention to a greater blessing.

Hearing God's word is a privilege.

But only those who hear, remember and follow it as their rule of life are truly blessed by the Lord.

Jesus warns those who demand signs (verses 29–36)

Jesus promised the sign of Jonah, which Matthew explains in relation to Christ's resurrection.

Even if Jesus himself preached constantly and worked miracles every day in a congregation, the hearers would not profit unless divine grace humbled their hearts.

Do not demand more signs or teaching than God has chosen to give.

Rather, pray for opened hearts and understanding so that the light already received will benefit us.

Beware especially that your supposed light is not really darkness.

Wrong governing principles will corrupt both judgment and conduct.

Jesus rebukes the Pharisees (verses 37–54)

We must examine our hearts and seek to have them cleansed and renewed.

While fulfilling the great demands of the law and gospel, we must not overlook smaller duties God has commanded.

When others watch our words, seeking an excuse to trap us, Lord, give us prudence and patience.

Defeat their malicious purposes, and grant us meekness enough to bear insults for Christ with joy, resting under the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Verses 1-4
"Lord, teach us to pray," is a good prayer, and a very needful one, for Jesus Christ only can teach us, by his word and Spirit, how to pray. Lord, teach me what it is to pray; Lord, stir up and quicken me to the duty; Lord, direct me what to pray for; teach me what I should say. Christ taught them a prayer, much the same that he had given before in his sermon upon the mount. There are some differences in the words of the Lord's prayer in Matthew and in Luke, but they are of no moment. Let us in our requests, both for others and for ourselves, come to our heavenly Father, confiding in his power and goodness.
[Luke.11.5-Luke.11.13]
Verses 5-13
Christ encourages fervency and constancy in prayer. We must come for what we need, as a man does to his neighbour or friend, who is kind to him. We must come for bread; for that which is needful. If God does not answer our prayers speedily, yet he will in due time, if we continue to pray. Observe what to pray for; we must ask for the Holy Spirit, not only as necessary in order to our praying well, but as all spiritual blessings are included in that one. For by the influences of the Holy Spirit we are brought to know God and ourselves, to repent, believe in, and love Christ, and so are made comfortable in this world, and meet for happiness in the next. All these blessings our heavenly Father is more ready to bestow on every one that asks for them, than an indulgent parent is to give food to a hungry child. And this is the advantage of the prayer of faith, that it quiets and establishes the heart in God.
[Luke.11.14-Luke.11.26]
Verses 14-26
Christ's thus casting out the devils, was really the destroying of their power. The heart of every unconverted sinner is the devil's palace, where he dwells, and where he rules. There is a kind of peace in the heart of an unconverted soul, while the devil, as a strong man armed, keeps it. The sinner is secure, has no doubt concerning the goodness of his state, nor any dread of the judgment to come. But observe the wonderful change made in conversion. The conversion of a soul to God, is Christ's victory over the devil and his power in that soul, restoring the soul to its liberty, and recovering his own interest in it and power over it. All the endowments of mind of body are now employed for Christ. Here is the condition of a hypocrite. The house is swept from common sins, by a forced confession, as Pharaoh's; by a feigned contrition, as Ahab's; or by a partial reformation, as Herod's. The house is swept, but it is not washed; the heart is not made holy. Sweeping takes off only the loose dirt, while the sin that besets the sinner, the beloved sin, is untouched. The house is garnished with common gifts and graces. It is not furnished with any true grace; it is all paint and varnish, not real nor lasting. It was never given up to Christ, nor dwelt in by the Spirit. Let us take heed of resting in that which a man may have, and yet come short of heaven. The wicked spirits enter in without any difficulty; they are welcomed, and they dwell there; there they work, there they rule. From such an awful state let all earnestly pray to be delivered.
[Luke.11.27-Luke.11.28]
Verses 27-28
While the scribes and Pharisees despised and blasphemed the discourses of our Lord Jesus, this good woman admired them, and the wisdom and power with which he spake. Christ led the woman to a higher consideration. Though it is a great privilege to hear the word of God, yet those only are truly blessed, that is, blessed of the Lord, that hear it, keep it in memory, and keep to it as their way and rule.
[Luke.11.29-Luke.11.36]
Verses 29-36
Christ promised that there should be one sign more given, even the sign of Jonah the prophet; which in Matthew is explained, as meaning the resurrection of Christ; and he warned them to improve this sign. But though Christ himself were the constant preacher in any congregation, and worked miracles daily among them, yet unless his grace humbled their hearts, they would not profit by his word. Let us not desire more evidence and fuller teaching than the Lord is pleased to afford us. We should pray without ceasing that our hearts and understandings may be opened, that we may profit by the light we enjoy. And especially take heed that the light which is in us be not darkness; for if our leading principles be wrong, our judgment and practice must become more so.
[Luke.11.37-Luke.11.54]
Verses 37-54
We should all look to our hearts, that they may be cleansed and new-created; and while we attend to the great things of the law and of the gospel, we must not neglect the smallest matter God has appointed. When any wait to catch something out of our mouths, that they may insnare us, O Lord, give us thy prudence and thy patience, and disappoint their evil purposes. Furnish us with such meekness and patience that we may glory in reproaches, for Christ's sake, and that thy Holy Spirit may rest upon us.

Jesus warns against denial and hypocrisy (verses 1–12)

Faith in God's universal providence should support us in danger and help us continue trusting him as we perform our duty.

God notices even sparrows and their smallest concerns. He therefore watches over the least interests of his disciples.

Those who acknowledge Jesus now will be acknowledged by him before God's angels at the final judgment.

Those who deny him to protect their life or gain worldly power will ultimately suffer a far greater loss: Christ will not acknowledge them.

But a trembling believer who has fallen and genuinely repents need not doubt the possibility of forgiveness.

That differs entirely from the hardened, determined hostility toward the Holy Spirit which, as Henry explains, is not forgiven because it is not repented of.

Greed and the rich fool (verses 13–21)

Christ's kingdom is spiritual, not an earthly empire.

Henry says Christianity does not seek political rule as its reward. It requires everyone to act justly, but does not promise worldly power or wealth as the advantage of receiving grace.

The benefits promised to Christ's disciples are of a higher kind.

We constantly need warning against greed.

Wealth cannot provide true happiness, comfort or satisfaction to a soul.

The rich fool was a clever manager of worldly affairs but neglected God's providence, life's uncertainty, the value of his soul and eternity.

Even professing believers sometimes hold up such worldly-minded people as models to imitate.

Our thoughts are not hidden from God.

When the man's land produced abundantly, instead of thanking the Lord and rejoicing that he could do more good, he was troubled: What shall I do now?

The poorest beggar could scarcely have spoken with greater anxiety.

Possessing more often creates more cares.

The man intended to use his abundance only for bodily pleasure, not to help others.

God would require his soul from him and call him to account.

What folly to pursue benefits for the body and for a few years while neglecting the soul and eternity!

Jesus calls his little flock away from anxiety (verses 22–40)

Jesus repeatedly warned against anxious, tormenting care for earthly things (Matthew 6:25–34).

Cast your cares on God, for this is the way to find peace.

Just as worry cannot change our height, it cannot give us sovereign control over our circumstances.

We should accept our situation under God's care instead of endlessly chasing worldly comforts.

Even necessary material things become harmful when pursued in panic and excessive worry.

Do not imagine every future disaster and invent needless cares in trying to prevent it.

If we value holiness, we will not be ruled by a desire for luxury.

Examine whether we belong to Christ's little flock.

He is our Master, and we are both working servants and waiting servants.

Remain ready to meet him, as household servants waiting late into the night for their master's return.

Henry connects this with Jesus' ascension, his summons to each believer through death, and his future return to judge the world.

Because the hour is unknown, remain prepared like someone guarding a house when a thief may arrive.

Watchfulness despite division (verses 41–53)

Everyone must apply Jesus' warnings personally.

Each person knows many wrong things they should avoid and many right duties they neglect. Ignorance therefore leaves no one without responsibility.

The gospel's spread would cause division and suffering.

That does not mean Christianity itself is violent or hostile; it is pure, peaceful and loving.

Conflict arises because its truth contradicts people's pride and sinful desires.

Before the gospel could be proclaimed widely, Jesus had a baptism of suffering and death to undergo—very different from baptism with water or the Spirit.

We should eagerly make the truth known even if it causes disagreement or opposition within families.

Through that witness people are converted and God receives glory.

Seek reconciliation while there is time (verses 54–59)

People should show the same practical wisdom about their souls that they show in ordinary affairs.

Hasten to make peace with God before it is too late.

When conscience tells us that our sin has set us against the Lord, come to him as God reconciling the world to himself through Christ.

While we are alive, we are still on the way, and this is the time to receive his mercy.

Verses 1-12
A firm belief of the doctrine of God's universal providence, and the extent of it, would satisfy us when in peril, and encourage us to trust God in the way of duty. Providence takes notice of the meanest creatures, even of the sparrows, and therefore of the smallest interests of the disciples of Christ. Those who confess Christ now, shall be owned by him in the great day, before the angels of God. To deter us from denying Christ, and deserting his truths and ways, we are here assured that those who deny Christ, though they may thus save life itself, and though they may gain a kingdom by it, will be great losers at last; for Christ will not know them, will not own them, nor show them favour. But let no trembling, penitent backslider doubt of obtaining forgiveness. This is far different from the determined enmity that is blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, which shall never be forgiven, because it will never be repented of.
[Luke.12.13-Luke.12.21]
Verses 13-21
Christ's kingdom is spiritual, and not of this world. Christianity does not meddle with politics; it obliges all to do justly, but wordly dominion is not founded in grace. It does not encourage expectations of worldly advantages by religion. The rewards of Christ's disciples are of another nature. Covetousness is a sin we need constantly to be warned against; for happiness and comfort do not depend on the wealth of this world. The things of the world will not satisfy the desires of a soul. Here is a parable, which shows the folly of carnal worldling while they live, and their misery when they die. The character drawn is exactly that of a prudent, worldly man, who has no grateful regard to the providence of God, nor any right thought of the uncertainty of human affairs, the worth of his soul, or the importance of eternity. How many, even among professed Christians, point out similar characters as models for imitation, and proper persons to form connexions with! We mistake if we think that thoughts are hid, and thoughts are free. When he saw a great crop upon his ground, instead of thanking God for it, or rejoicing to be able to do more good, he afflicts himself. What shall I do now? The poorest beggar in the country could not have said a more anxious word. The more men have, the more perplexity they have with it. It was folly for him to think of making no other use of his plenty, than to indulge the flesh and gratify the sensual appetites, without any thought of doing good to others. Carnal worldlings are fools; and the day is coming when God will call them by their own name, and they will call themselves so. The death of such persons is miserable in itself, and terrible to them. Thy soul shall be required. He is loth to part with it; but God shall require it, shall require an account of it, require it as a guilty soul to be punished without delay. It is the folly of most men, to mind and pursue that which is for the body and for time only, more than that for the soul and eternity.
[Luke.12.22-Luke.12.40]
Verses 22-40
Christ largely insisted upon this caution not to give way to disquieting, perplexing cares, [Matt.6.25-Matt.6.34] Mt 6:25-34. The arguments here used are for our encouragement to cast our care upon God, which is the right way to get ease. As in our stature, so in our state, it is our wisdom to take it as it is. An eager, anxious pursuit of the things of this world, even necessary things, ill becomes the disciples of Christ. Fears must not prevail; when we frighten ourselves with thoughts of evil to come, and put ourselves upon needless cares how to avoid it. If we value the beauty of holiness, we shall not crave the luxuries of life. Let us then examine whether we belong to this little flock. Christ is our Master, and we are his servants; not only working servants, but waiting servants. We must be as men that wait for their lord, that sit up while he stays out late, to be ready to receive him. In this Christ alluded to his own ascension to heaven, his coming to call his people to him by death, and his return to judge the world. We are uncertain as to the time of his coming to us, we should therefore be always ready. If men thus take care of their houses, let us be thus wise for our souls. Be ye therefore ready also; as ready as the good man of the house would be, if he knew at what hour the thief would come.
[Luke.12.41-Luke.12.53]
Verses 41-53
All are to take to themselves what Christ says in his word, and to inquire concerning it. No one is left so ignorant as not to know many things to be wrong which he does, and many things to be right which he neglects; therefore all are without excuse in their sin. The bringing in the gospel dispensation would occasion desolations. Not that this would be the tendency of Christ's religion, which is pure, peaceable, and loving; but the effect of its being contrary to men's pride and lusts. There was to be a wide publication of the gospel. But before that took place, Christ had a baptism to be baptized with, far different from that of water and the Holy Spirit. He must endure sufferings and death. It agreed not with his plan to preach the gospel more widely, till this baptism was completed. We should be zealous in making known the truth, for though divisions will be stirred up, and a man's own household may be his foes, yet sinners will be converted, and God will be glorified.
[Luke.12.54-Luke.12.59]
Verses 54-59
Christ would have the people to be as wise in the concerns of their souls as they are in outward affairs. Let them hasten to obtain peace with God before it is too late. If any man has found that God has set himself against him concerning his sins, let him apply to him as God in Christ reconciling the world to himself. While we are alive, we are in the way, and now is our time.

Verses 1-5
Mention was made to Christ of the death of some Galileans. This tragical story is briefly related here, and is not met with in any historians. In Christ's reply he spoke of another event, which, like it, gave an instance of people taken away by sudden death. Towers, that are built for safety, often prove to be men's destruction. He cautioned his hearers not to blame great sufferers, as if they were therefore to be accounted great sinners. As no place or employment can secure from the stroke of death, we should consider the sudden removals of others as warnings to ourselves. On these accounts Christ founded a call to repentance. The same Jesus that bids us repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand, bids us repent, for otherwise we shall perish.
[Luke.13.6-Luke.13.9]
Verses 6-9
This parable of the barren fig-tree is intended to enforce the warning given just before: the barren tree, except it brings forth fruit, will be cut down. This parable in the first place refers to the nation and people of the Jews. Yet it is, without doubt, for awakening all that enjoy the means of grace, and the privileges of the visible church. When God has borne long, we may hope that he will bear with us yet a little longer, but we cannot expect that he will bear always.
[Luke.13.10-Luke.13.17]
Verses 10-17
Our Lord Jesus attended upon public worship on the sabbaths. Even bodily infirmities, unless very grievous, should not keep us from public worship on sabbath days. This woman came to Christ to be taught, and to get good to her soul, and then he relieved her bodily infirmity. This cure represents the work of Christ's grace upon the soul. And when crooked souls are made straight, they will show it by glorifying God. Christ knew that this ruler had a real enmity to him and to his gospel, and that he did but cloak it with a pretended zeal for the sabbath day; he really would not have them be healed any day; but if Jesus speaks the word, and puts forth his healing power, sinners are set free. This deliverance is often wrought on the Lord's day; and whatever labour tends to put men in the way of receiving the blessing, agrees with the design of that day.
[Luke.13.18-Luke.13.22]
Verses 18-22
Here is the progress of the gospel foretold in two parables, as in Mt 13. The kingdom of the Messiah is the kingdom of God. May grace grow in our hearts; may our faith and love grow exceedingly, so as to give undoubted evidence of their reality. May the example of God's saints be blessed to those among whom they live; and may his grace flow from heart to heart, until the little one becomes a thousand.
[Luke.13.23-Luke.13.30]
Verses 23-30
Our Saviour came to guide men's consciences, not to gratify their curiosity. Ask not, How many shall be saved? But, Shall I be one of them? Not, What shall become of such and such? But, What shall I do, and what will become of me? Strive to enter in at the strait gate. This is directed to each of us; it is, Strive ye. All that will be saved, must enter in at the strait gate, must undergo a change of the whole man. Those that would enter in, must strive to enter. Here are awakening considerations, to enforce this exhortation. Oh that we may be all awakened by them! They answer the question, Are there few that shall be saved? But let none despond either as to themselves or others, for there are last who shall be first, and first who shall be last. If we reach heaven, we shall meet many there whom we little thought to meet, and miss many whom we expected to find.
[Luke.13.31-Luke.13.35]
Verses 31-35
Christ, in calling Herod a fox, gave him his true character. The greatest of men were accountable to God, therefore it became him to call this proud king by his own name; but it is not an example for us. I know, said our Lord, that I must die very shortly; when I die, I shall be perfected, I shall have completed my undertaking. It is good for us to look upon the time we have before us as but little, that we may thereby be quickened to do the work of the day in its day. The wickedness of persons and places which more than others profess religion and relation to God, especially displeases and grieves the Lord Jesus. The judgment of the great day will convince unbelievers; but let us learn thankfully to welcome, and to profit by all who come in the name of the Lord, to call us to partake of his great salvation.

Jesus heals on the Sabbath (verses 1–6)

The Pharisee who hosted Jesus seems to have intended harm by inviting him, as others had done.

Yet Jesus did not refuse to heal the sick man simply because opponents would object to his actions on the Sabbath.

We must carefully distinguish the demands of piety and charity, the work of genuine necessity and habits of selfish indulgence.

True wisdom from above teaches us to continue patiently in doing good.

Jesus teaches humility and generosity (verses 7–14)

Jesus notices our behavior even in ordinary daily activities.

He watches us not only during worship but also around our tables.

Human pride often brings a person low, while humility prepares the way for lasting honor.

Christ teaches us that practical charity is better than a show of importance.

He did not mean that proud people who give generously without faith can demand a reward from God.

Rather, he calls us to help poor and afflicted people from love for him.

The great banquet (verses 15–24)

This parable displays the free grace and mercy of God through Christ's gospel.

To people who recognize their spiritual poverty and misery, the gospel provides food and a feast for the soul.

The invited guests all found some excuse for staying away.

Henry applies the initial rejection to the Jewish nation's neglect of Christ's gracious invitation.

It also exposes the reluctance present in the human heart to accept the gospel.

People who reject the offer are ungrateful, treating the God of heaven with contempt and provoking his righteous anger.

When the invitation was refused, the apostles were sent to the Gentiles, and the church was filled with people from the nations.

God has not prepared the gospel's rich provision in vain.

If some refuse it, others will thankfully accept.

The poor and socially insignificant are as welcome to Christ as the wealthy and powerful.

Indeed, the gospel often prospers especially among those suffering poverty, disability or other worldly disadvantages.

At last Christ's house will be full, when the number of his elect people is complete.

Count the cost of following Jesus (verses 25–35)

Not every disciple of Christ will be crucified, but every disciple must bear a cross while performing the duties of faith.

Jesus commands us to expect this and carefully consider it.

The illustration of building a tower teaches us to count the expense of our discipleship.

The illustration of a king considering battle teaches us to weigh its dangers.

The cost includes putting sin to death, even the sinful desires we love most.

Even the boldest sinner cannot withstand God when he judges.

Who can measure the power of his anger?

Our true interest is to seek peace with him.

We need not send to discover his terms of peace; he has already offered them, and they are wholly for our good.

Every believer's faith will be tested in some form.

Now that Zacchaeus had turned from sin to God, he was truly blessed.

Christ had entered his home, and where he comes he brings salvation.

Everyone who has received a gift must use it in serving others (1 Peter 4:10).

Christ calls his servants to account for the opportunities entrusted to them.

The parable also warns of the punishment awaiting those openly hostile to him and those who profess loyalty without genuine service.

Henry notes a distinction between the two parables:

The single mina given to each servant suggests the one gospel offered equally to all who hear it.

The different numbers of talents suggest the varied abilities and advantages through which people may make use of that same gospel.

Christ rules all creatures and can use them as he pleases.

He knows every human heart and holds it within his sovereign power.

Jesus' triumphal entry and his disciples' joyful praise angered the proud Pharisees, who opposed him and his kingdom.

He refuses to be discouraged by the contempt of proud people but welcomes the praises of the humble.

The Pharisees wished to silence those praising him.

He wept over Jerusalem, and terrible judgment later fell upon it.

The Son of God did not weep for himself or over something trivial.

He knew the value of souls and the heavy weight of human guilt.

May he cleanse our hearts from every corruption through his Spirit.

Jesus' authority is challenged (verses 1–8)

Some people claim to be investigating the evidence for revelation and the truth of the gospel, when they are really looking for excuses to continue in unbelief.

Jesus responded to the priests and scribes with a simple question about John's baptism.

Ordinary people could have answered it.

They knew John's ministry came from heaven and aimed at spiritual rather than worldly ends.

When people bury the knowledge already given to them, it is right that they should be denied further understanding.

The religious leaders refused to acknowledge what they knew.

Jesus therefore rightly declined to explain his own authority to people who would not accept the divine origin of John's mission.

The tenants of the vineyard (verses 9–19)

Jesus addressed the parable to people determined to reject his authority despite abundant evidence for it.

How many still resemble those who killed the prophets and ultimately crucified Christ!

Their hostility to God springs from a desire to live according to sinful passions without being restrained.

Everyone privileged to possess God's word should use that blessing faithfully.

The judgment will be terrible for those who reject the Son.

It will also come upon those who claim to honor him but fail to produce the fruits of obedience in due season.

The hearers recognized that the punishment in the parable was just.

Yet they could not bear to hear its application to themselves.

Sinners often persevere in a destructive path even while fearing its final consequences.

Paying taxes and giving God what belongs to him (verses 20–26)

People plotting against Christ and his gospel cannot hide their motives from him.

Jesus refused to be trapped into the false choice his questioners presented.

He exposed their dishonest intention without giving them a statement that would allow them to turn either the governor or the people against him.

Wisdom from heaven can guide those who sincerely teach God's way around traps laid by malicious people.

It also clarifies our duties toward God, civil rulers and other human beings.

By faithfully fulfilling those duties, we prevent opponents from making justified accusations against us.

Jesus answers the Sadducees about resurrection (verses 27–38)

People seeking to undermine God's truth often create artificial difficulties and then treat them as decisive objections.

We mislead ourselves and misrepresent Christ's teaching when we imagine the unseen future world must operate exactly like the visible present world.

There is a world we see now, and a world still unseen.

Consider both carefully and give your greatest attention to the one that matters most.

Believers will share in the blessed resurrection of the dead.

We cannot fully imagine or describe their future happiness (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Those who enter their Lord's joy are entirely occupied with him.

Where holiness is perfect, the restraints needed against sin here are no longer necessary.

God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

He was fully sufficient for them (Genesis 17:1) and their exceeding great reward (Genesis 15:1).

Yet their earthly lives did not receive everything embraced in those promises.

There must therefore be another life in which God fulfills the full extent of his covenant commitment to them.

Jesus silences the scribes (verses 39–47)

Some scribes praised Jesus' answer about resurrection.

Yet his question about the Messiah silenced them.

Christ as God is David's Lord; Christ as man is David's descendant.

Jesus warned that scribes who exploited poor widows would face severe judgment.

They also misused religious practices, especially prayer, to conceal worldly and wicked schemes.

Hypocritical devotion adds another sin to wrongdoing.

Let us ask God to keep us from pride, ambition, greed and every other evil.

May he teach us to seek the honor that comes from him alone.
